article.title: The Trump Shock That Wasn’t (At Least Not Yet)

metadata_extension.subtitle: The “core” U.S. trade deficit is still expanding, thanks to strong electronics imports.

summary.central_question: Why has the large shock to trade rules from Trump's tariffs produced only a small shock to core trade flows so far?
summary.main_thesis: The tariff shock to trade rules has been far larger than the shock to trade flows, at least so far.

content.text: Why has the large shock to trade rules from Trump's tariffs produced only a small shock to core trade flows so far?
content.reason: A shift in policy regime need not show up immediately in the quantities it is meant to affect.

passages.source_excerpt: The impact of the tariffs core trade flows—and hence the global economy—has been modest, at least so far.

content.text: The U.S. moved from low, bound, most-favoured-nation tariffs to high, unbound, country-specific tariffs with demanding rules of origin, a rejection of WTO rules for all trade.
content.reason: Abandoning non-discrimination and binding commitments is a regime change, whatever the trade outcome.

passages.source_excerpt: The U.S. has gone from low-bound tariffs

content.text: Tariff rates now range from 50% for India and Brazil to 10% for Australia and the UK, with zero for USMCA-compliant trade.
content.reason: Divergent rates by origin for the same good measure the departure from equal treatment.

passages.source_excerpt: Importers of the same good will pay different tariffs depending on the origin of the good (50 percent for India and Brazil, 30 percent for China

content.text: Import swings exceeded those of COVID or Lehman, with the annualized deficit going from $2 trillion to $1 trillion and back to about $1.2 trillion, where it began.
content.reason: Headline trade volatility must be checked against its starting point before it is read as a lasting change.

passages.source_excerpt: The annualized monthly trade deficit rose to a peak of $2 trillion in March before dipping to $1 trillion and then rebounding to $1.2 trillion in July

content.text: The headline volatility comes from pharmaceutical stockpiling and tax-driven trade, and from gold flows, not from core trade.
content.reason: Tax-driven and financial flows can swamp trade aggregates without reflecting real demand.

passages.source_excerpt: pharmaceuticals (where trade is heavily distorted by tax and companies can easily front-run tariffs by stockpiling active ingredients) and gold.

content.text: Core trade is measured excluding pharmaceuticals and gold, and on that basis it looks normal.
content.reason: Strip out distorted categories to see the underlying trend.

passages.source_excerpt: Take out pharmaceuticals and gold and U.S. trade looks, well, rather normal.

content.text: Gold and pharmaceutical flows say little about real economic activity or global demand, so leaving them out reveals the true tariff effect.
content.reason: Excluding categories is valid only if they are noise with respect to the question asked.

content.text: Imports from China fell but imports from Taiwan and Southeast Asia soared, leaving total imports from Asia about flat.
content.reason: Bilateral declines can be offset by diversion to other sources.

passages.source_excerpt: imports from China (where hefty tariffs were expected) tanked. But imports from Taiwan and Southeast Asia

content.text: Bilateral tariffs mainly reroute trade through relocated final assembly rather than reducing total imports or Chinese content.
content.reason: Discriminatory tariffs invite trade diversion when rules of origin are loose.

passages.source_excerpt: firms shifted final assembly to southeast Asia to get around the bilateral tariffs

content.text: Tariffs have slowed auto imports, and importers waiting for tariff relief will depress them further in September.
content.reason: Expected changes in tariffs shift the timing of imports.

passages.source_excerpt: expect a big dip in September as European and Japanese importers wait for the finalization of their “deals”

content.text: An AI data-center investment boom has pushed electronics imports up, with imports from Taiwan more than 50% higher year to date.
content.reason: Strong domestic investment demand can outweigh tariff price effects on imports.

passages.source_excerpt: imports of electronics are up substantially (imports from Taiwan are up over 50 percent YTD) on the back of booming investment in data centers

content.text: Global trade has held up well despite the U.S. flouting the rules.
content.reason: Aggregate trade resilience is judged by core flows, not by headline swings.

passages.source_excerpt: So global trade has actually held up rather well even though the world’s largest economy

content.text: Record U.S. tariff revenue signals that imports continue and Americans are bearing the tariff.
content.reason: Tariff revenue is the rate times the volume, so high revenue means volumes have not collapsed.

passages.source_excerpt: the surge in revenue implies that Americans are continuing to import and just paying the tariff.

content.text: The import response to a broad price change such as an exchange rate move is about 0.3 to 0.4.
content.reason: A broad tariff acts on import prices much like a currency depreciation.

passages.source_excerpt: The import elasticity for exchange rate moves is closer to 0.3 or 0.4

content.text: The elasticity of about 2 seen in the first-term China tariffs overstates the effect of a global tariff, because it reflects diversion.
content.reason: Elasticities estimated from bilateral shocks include substitution that is unavailable when tariffs are universal.

passages.source_excerpt: the bilateral tariff elasticity of 2 is too high for a global tariff increase

content.reason: Past episodes calibrate expected tariff responses.

content.text: A roughly 15% tariff wall should cut imports by 5 to 6%, taking non-oil imports from about 10% to about 9.5% of GDP: meaningful, but far smaller than COVID or the financial crisis.
content.reason: The expected volume effect is the price change times the elasticity.

passages.source_excerpt: so a 15 percent tariff might be expected to reduce impacts by 5-6 percent. That is a year or two of normal import volume growth

content.text: Foreign exporters can offset lost U.S. sales by taking market share from U.S. exporters burdened by tariffed inputs.
content.reason: Tariffs on inputs tax a country's own exports.

passages.source_excerpt: Some countries will be able to offset reduced U.S. sales by taking market share from US exports

content.text: Unlike a tariff, a real depreciation also raises exports, because export price elasticities are higher.
content.reason: The analogy between a tariff and a depreciation holds only on the import side.

passages.source_excerpt: An actual exchange rate depreciation increases exports as well as lowering imports

content.reason: Compare the actual data with the predicted effect.

content.text: The tariff shock to trade rules has been far larger than the shock to trade flows, at least so far.
content.reason: Judge a policy shock by its measured real effects as well as its legal form.

passages.source_excerpt: The liberation day shock to the trade rules was thus bigger than the shock to overall trade flows.

content.text: The fall data, after the August tariff hikes, should show a larger impact than is visible now.
content.reason: Tariff effects arrive with a lag and must be reassessed as data comes in.

passages.source_excerpt: Let’s though see what judgement day brings, and what the data for the fall shows—there should be more of an impact than is now apparent.

content.text: The verdict may not hold, because the August deals raised tariffs sharply and their effects are not yet in the data.
content.reason: Recent policy changes are not yet captured in current data.

passages.source_excerpt: The August deals and letters resulted in hefty tariff increases for many countries (tariffs on Southeast Asia doubled relative to April).

content.text: A tariff left in place is passed through to import prices and persists long enough to change trade volumes.
content.reason: Elasticity-based forecasts require that the price change persists and reaches buyers.
